learning_outcomes.text: Acquire the methods and knowledge on the main classes of ferrous metals (steels and cast iron) and light alloys (Aluminum, Magnesium) with emphasis on the relationship between mechanical properties and microstructure.
Apply knowledge acquired in a real context of industrial issues through practical classroom or laboratory exercises.

Comprehend and critically evaluate the alloying elements in the major classes of studied metals, thermal treatments, microstructure, mechanical and physical characteristics and main applications, to give guidance on the design choice of the metallic material.

Acquire the specific vocabulary inherent in physical metallurgy and the main classes of ferrous and non-ferrous metals, and be able to transmit the content of the course and metallurgical problems in oral and written form.

Deepen knowledge in the metallurgical field through the autonomous consultation of specialized texts, scientific or divulgative journals, even outside the subjects strictly dealt with in lesson, in order to effectively address insertion in the world of work or undertake further training paths.

syllabus_topics: Fundamental physical metallurgy: solidification of metals, defects, diffusion and thermal treatments
Microstructure and mechanical characterisation of metals: tensile tests, light and electron microscopy
Non-ferrous metals and light alloys: general issues
Aluminum and its alloys: designation, casting alloys, wrought alloys
Case studies and criteria for selecting metallic materials based on applications
assessment_rules: The exam is passed if the grade is at least 18/30. The grade '30 cum laude' is given if the maximum score is achieved and mastery of the disciplinary vocabulary is demonstrated.
bibliography: I.J. Polmear, Light alloys –Metallurgy of the Light Metals, 3 ed.Butterworth-Heinemann, Oxford (2000)
